title: Comparative Deployment Scenarios and Tradeoffs — Pocketbook for Technical Buyers
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

Purpose: A concise, field-ready reference for technical buyers (platform engineers, infra architects, CTOs) that compares common inference deployment patterns, surfaces predictable tradeoffs across latency/cost/privacy, and provides repeatable pilot and pitch artifacts tailored to Redwood Inference. Use this pocketbook during discovery calls, architect briefings, and pilot scoping.

Audience: Technical buyers evaluating inference platforms, solution architects building deployment proposals, sales engineers running pilots.

Executive summary:
- Redwood supports three primary deployment modes: Hosted (Redwood API), Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), Private (VPC / on-prem). Each mode targets distinct risk and economics profiles.
- This document distills the business and technical tradeoffs and provides sample language, a pricing compass, a one-page pilot checklist, a compact competitive brief, and a short security FAQ for prospect-level conversations.

1) Quick comparative table (single-page cheat)

| Scenario | Best for | Typical 99th Pct Latency SLO | Estimated cost per 1M tokens (USD) | Primary risks | Redwood differentiation |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Hosted (API) | Early experimentation, PLG usage, dev velocity | 180–400 ms | $120–$600 | Data residency, multi-tenant concerns for regulated data | Fast onboarding, streaming, curated model catalog |
| Dedicated (reserved) | High-throughput apps with predictable budgets | 40–150 ms | $80–$350 (with reserved commits) | Over/under provisioning; capacity planning | Reserved capacity, autoscale policies, SLA-backed latency targets |
| Private (VPC / on-prem) | Regulated workloads, air-gapped environments | 30–120 ms (hardware dependent) | $70–$500 (hardware + ops vary widely) | Ops burden, hardware procurement, long lead times | Private control plane, KMS/HSM integrations, on-prem packaging |

Notes: latency ranges are illustrative for typical LLM sequence lengths (256–512 tokens) using mainstream GPUs (A100/4090 variants). Cost estimates combine model runtime, batching efficiency, and amortized infra. Always run a short pilot to validate with customer-specific token distribution.

2) Messaging and positioning framework (talking points)

Top-line claim: "Make inference predictable — choose the deployment that matches your risk and economics, and iterate with the same API across hosted, dedicated, and private modes."

For platform engineers:
- Emphasize: identical API and rollout controls across modes, model pinning, and tracing hooks for root-cause analysis.
- Evidence: token-level cost breakdowns and per-route latency histograms in Redwood Console.

For security/compliance stakeholders:
- Emphasize: private control plane option, customer-managed KMS, audit logs, and SOC2-ready processes.
- Evidence: deployment-specific evidence packet (appendix link) and sample contractual language for DPA/SLA.

For finance/ops:
- Emphasize: reserved capacity for predictable unit economics and Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization which reduce per-token cost.
- Evidence: pilot ROI model (see Pilot Economics section).

3) Compact competitive brief (one paragraph each)

- Major cloud managed endpoints: Good for VM-level control; weaker on model-aware batching, inference-oriented kernel selection, and developer ergonomics for rollouts. Redwood offers inference-first runtime optimizations and transparent per-token economics.
- LLM API-only providers: Strong in simplicity, but often limited in private deployment and observability. Redwood matches API simplicity while providing Dedicated/Private variants and deep cost tooling.
- Self-hosted runtimes: Offer full control but require significant ops investment. Redwood Private reduces that lift with packaging, automated upgrade/rollback playbooks, and a private control plane option.

4) Sample 6-slide pitch deck outline (for SEs)

Slide 1 — One-liner + logo\- "Predictable inference economics and SLOs for production LLM features."
Slide 2 — Problem statements (cost unpredictability, model regressions, slow rollouts)
Slide 3 — Redwood solution (modes + runtime + Console) with a small architecture diagram (textual: request routing -> runtime -> KV cache -> trace/logs -> cost dashboards)
Slide 4 — Decision matrix (latency vs cost vs control) populated from the table above
Slide 5 — Pilot ask & measurement plan (sample success metrics below)
Slide 6 — Security & compliance evidence + next steps (POC/contract timeline)

Speaker notes (short): Always open with the customer's primary constraint and then map to one mode. For example: "If your blocker is predictability & SLA, consider Dedicated with a 6-month reserved commit. If it's data residency, Private is the shortest path to compliance."

5) Pricing compass & pilot economics (how to frame numbers)

Guiding principle: anchor to a pilot-sized workload and extrapolate. Avoid claiming hard numbers without a live trace.

Sample pilot model (template language for calls):
- Pilot scope: 2–4 endpoints, 10k–50k requests/day, sequence length 128–512 tokens.
- Est. hosted cost (pilot): $1,000–$6,000/month depending on model family and streaming usage.
- Est. dedicated (reserved 3-month): unit cost improvement typically 20–60% vs hosted at scale, depending on burst profile and batching.

ROI examples (framing language):
- "Customer A moved from ad-hoc GPUs to Dedicated and saw a 46% reduction in per-token bill via increased batching and prefix cache reuse over a 90-day baseline."
- Use Redwood Optimize suggestions during pilot to validate quantization and batching levers.

6) One-page pilot checklist (operational)

Pre-pilot (1 week):
1) Agree on sample workload and traffic trace (token distribution + sequences).
2) Choose pilot mode (Hosted small, or Dedicated trial).
3) Exchange basic security artifacts (IP allowlist, DPA).
4) Provision accounts and access; share API key / role for SEs.

Pilot execution (2–4 weeks):
1) Baseline run: run 3–5 days of production-like traffic through Redwood API and capture metrics.
2) Enable Console tracing and token-level breakdown; validate latency SLOs.
3) Implement Optimize recommendations (batching, KV caching) and measure delta.
4) Validate model-output quality against agreed prompt set (sample evals).

Success criteria (example):
- Latency: 99th Pct < agreed SLO (e.g., 200 ms for hosted pilot).
- Cost: projected per-token unit cost reduction >= 25% when extrapolated to target traffic profile.
- Quality: no >5% degradation on core prompt-set precision metrics.

Post-pilot (contract/scale):
1) Deliver pilot report with economics, recommended config, and roll-out plan.
2) If Dedicated desired: propose capacity commit and SLA. If Private: supply packaging and on-prem timeline.

7) Security FAQ (concise answers for prospect-level questions)

Q: Where is customer data stored?
A: Hosted: transient persistence in our region-specific storage; customers may restrict regions. Dedicated/Private: customer data remains isolated in reserved pools or customer VPC.

Q: How is data encrypted?
A: In transit: TLS 1.2+/mTLS for private links. At rest: AES-256. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM; for Dedicated we offer KMS integration per contract.

Q: Do you provide audit logs?
A: Yes. Redwood Console exposes request/response tracing and an audit logging export (S3 or SIEM sinks). Logs can be configured for retention and redaction.

Q: Can we run Redwood in an air-gapped environment?
A: Yes — our on-prem packaging supports air-gapped installs. See the engineering playbook (link) for offline upgrade and dependency lists.

Q: What compliance evidence do you have?
A: Redwood maintains SOC 2 Type II, and we provide contract-level attestations plus a standard evidence packet for due diligence. Additional compliance work (e.g., FedRAMP) is available via enterprise engagement.

8) Mini-case study (two-paragraph, field script)

Customer: FinServeX (regional banking SaaS) — anonymized\Problem: Highly variable peak inference load for document summarization. Existing endpoint had unpredictable costs and occasional timeouts during peak business hours.
Solution: 8-week pilot using Dedicated with autoscale burst policy and KV prefix caching. SEs ran Optimize recommendations and validated model quantization tradeoffs on a held-out prompt set.

Outcome: FinServeX reduced effective per-token spend by 39% and improved 95th Pct latency from 1.2s to 340ms under peak load. The bank selected a 12-month reserved commit and integrated Redwood’s trace exports with their SIEM.

9) Objection-handling snippets (for SEs)

Objection: "We can just self-host; why pay?"
Response: "Self-hosting gives control but shifts engineering focus to runtime ops. Redwood private reduces that lift with packaging, automated upgrades, and expert support — you gain production-grade inference practices without a bespoke infra team."

Objection: "How do we trust latency at scale?"
Response: "We provide per-route dashboards, 99th Pct latency traces, and can run synthetic load tests during the pilot. Our Dedicated SLAs include latency targets for reserved pools."

10) Appendix: example API warming snippet (for SEs to share)

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \n  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <KEY>' \n  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \n  -d '{"model":"rwd-small-1","input":"Warm cache: <example prefix>","max_tokens":64}'

Tip: Use short, representative prefixes to populate KV caches during performance tests. Include a small burst ramp (10x) to validate autoscale behavior.
